2019-05-18_1: SFIO stated the complaint came with a bulky record in four boxes and that, besides those already arrested, 178 further accused were to be prosecuted. Court took the complaint on board subject to verification of the copies and record, and directed the Ahlmad to verify the documents before contentions were heard.
2019-05-28_1: SFIO stated that although prosecution of about 186 accused was sought, six names had been omitted from the list filed with the complaint. Court held the amendment merely corrected an inadvertent mistake in the title and allowed it, taking the amended list of accused and of witnesses on record.
2019-05-30_1: Defence sought exemption for Vivek Harivyasi on the plea of serious medical complications and hospitalisation, supported by medical records - allowed. Defence also pressed for a soft copy of the voluminous record; SFIO, on departmental instructions, stated no soft copy could be given, and the prayer was declined at that stage.
2019-06-03_2: Operative summoning order. SFIO stated it had already entered the entire data in soft form; the court used that to expedite matters, directing SFIO to prepare the warrants on a court-supplied proforma within 15 days for service through the DCP (Headquarters).
2019-06-03_3: The reasoned cognizance order. SFIO's case: the MCA ordered investigation into 125 Adarsh Group companies and LLPs under s.212(1)(c) Companies Act 2013; the investigation report of 09.05.2019 is deemed a police report under s.173 CrPC by virtue of s.212(15). The accused were categorised 1-5 by control and ownership. SFIO submitted that Mukesh Modi and his family and associates were in direct or indirect control of the corporate entities to the degree of being their 'directing mind and will', acting in connivance with the other accused; that 54 companies and their directors were liable under s.58A(5) of the 1956 Act for the period to 31.03.2014; and that Abhay K Shah & Associates was statutory auditor of the group with Abhay K Shah, Ichchhita Dungarwal and Neha Kataria as signing partners. Court found sufficient prima facie evidence against A-1 to A-187 and set out offence-wise liability.
2019-06-13_1: No defence contention. Court's own observation: the jail authorities should have required Jaipur police to seek this court's permission before transferring custody, and even on a production warrant the Rajasthan police were bound to produce the accused. Show cause notices issued to the SHO, SOG Jaipur and to the Superintendent, District Jail Gurugram.
2019-06-17_1: Jaipur police submitted the accused were on police remand from the CMM, Jaipur until 22.06.2019, that they could not be produced on 13.06.2019 due to unavoidable circumstances, and asked that custody remain with them for smooth investigation. The Jail Superintendent replied that custody had been handed to Haryana police who produced them before the CMM Jaipur, that prior permission is usually taken, and that no intentional omission occurred, regretting the inconvenience. Court kept the reply under consideration.
2019-07-01_1: Police explained non-production of accused on production warrants by want of sufficient police force; no explanation at all was offered for Mukesh Modi and Rahul Modi. Court recorded the absence of explanation and issued fresh production warrants.
2019-07-30_1: The first substantial contest on personal appearance. Bailable warrants were served but none of the accused appeared; instead they moved separate applications under s.205 CrPC seeking exemption on grounds of medical problems or personal reasons. SFIO opposed vehemently, calling the grounds false and fabricated. Court held that irrespective of the individual grounds there was no basis in fact or law for exemption, because the accused stood summoned for a non-bailable offence under the Companies Act 2013 triable as a warrant case; they were required to surrender and seek regular bail, and non-bailable warrants could even have been issued given the gravity of the allegations. SFIO also explained the group structures, so that A-1 to A-70 would be served through A-123, A-71 to A-78 through A-135, and the Harivyasi companies through A-115.
2019-08-13_1: Defence for Surender Singh (A-140) argued that Akshat Singh, the other director of the same companies A-81 and A-82, faced identical allegations, so his bail should await Akshat Singh's appearance; SFIO did not oppose and sought to verify issues. Court agreed that bail pleas within a set of companies would be similar and deciding one would affect the others, and adjourned. Another accused argued there was no summoning order against him under s.447 for violation of ss.73 and 74 read with the proviso to s.76-A. The core question identified for the group of bail applications was whether an offence under s.448 punishable under s.447 was made out against directors who had signed the account books without mala fide intention.
2019-09-04_1: Applicants sought interim protection pending their anticipatory bail applications. SFIO argued the accused had full knowledge of the summoning order and were intentionally avoiding service to delay the proceedings. Court reasoned that since the applicants had invoked s.438 and their applications were adjourned for reply, arrest in the meantime would render those applications infructuous; in the interest of a fair chance it directed that no coercive process issue until the bail applications were decided, expressly without any observation on merits. Separately, an exemption application was dismissed on the ground that the accused stood summoned for non-bailable offences in a serious economic fraud. Notice under s.446 CrPC issued to a surety who claimed he had merely signed the bonds as identifier.
2019-09-16_1: Defence produced the High Court's order of 13.09.2019 in CWP No.23904-2019 granting interim protection in the same terms as the Supreme Court's order in Vijay Shukla's case, and argued the arrest warrant therefore amounted to coercive process. Court accepted this and directed the warrant not be executed.
2019-09-16_2: SFIO alleged that Mukesh Modi (A-113), Rahul Modi (A-114) and Ishwar Singh Sindal (A-131) had been taken by Ahmedabad police and not returned to Central Jail, Jaipur. The Jail Superintendent's written reply blamed an ACMM Jaipur order; the court rejected it as baseless, observing the ACMM had never directed the jail not to produce the accused elsewhere and had no authority to prevent their production before a Special Court of a Sessions Judge.
2019-09-17_1: Six accused sought relaxation of the passport and travel conditions, arguing they were senior executives who must travel at short notice, that the condition impeded their duties, and that there was no prima facie evidence against them - a point the court had already observed when granting bail. SFIO conceded at the bar that as to these six it was essentially a case of no evidence. Court relaxed and recalled the passport and travel conditions.
2019-09-18_1: Both sides relied on new facts and case law against each other and jointly sought time to study the authorities before addressing arguments; adjourned, bail extended.
2019-09-18_2: SFIO applied to correct clerical errors in the summoning order of 03.06.2019, explaining that in Para 9 some names had been omitted and others wrongly inserted through a copy-paste error while repeatedly pasting names - in particular A-115 to A-141 omitted from sub-para (I), companies omitted from (V), A-122 omitted from (VI), A-154 wrongly substituted for A-126 in (VII). Court applied the principle that an error apparent on the face of the record does not depend for its discovery on argument or disputation, and that a clerical error is a mistake in writing or typing, and allowed the correction, the discussion in the order having carried the correct details of their roles throughout.
2019-09-18_3: Twelve anticipatory bail applications part-heard and directed to be decided simultaneously as arising from the same facts. On Nitin Rathore's (A-116) application to cancel his arrest warrant, counsel confirmed he was not surrendering but would join the trial when directed. Court dismissed it: if he had genuinely shifted address 5-6 years earlier, his knowledge of the pendency of the complaint was unexplained; that knowledge showed he was aware of the proceedings and the application was filed merely to gain time, and was not maintainable absent surrender.
2019-09-23_1: Part arguments heard in twelve anticipatory bail applications. Counsel for Shiv Raj Sharma sought a date because a similarly placed accused's petition was pending in the High Court on 27.09.2019, and SFIO sought time to clarify technical issues raised by the defence. Adjourned on joint request, with no further opportunity.
2019-09-27_1: Defence placed on record that the High Court on 26.09.2019 had fixed CWP No.23904 of 2019 and directed this court to decide the bail application on its merits, though the certified copy had not arrived. Court noted the arrest warrant already issued and the pending anticipatory bail, and directed the warrant not be executed till 04.10.2019, subject to further High Court directions.
2019-10-03_1: A run of exemption applications, contested. Aditya Sarda (A-141) pleaded viral fever; SFIO argued the application was not maintainable because a warrant of arrest had already issued, and the defence relied on Arunkumar N. Chaturvedi v. State of Maharashtra and Chundru Ammanna v. Asst. Commissioner of Labour on maintainability. Praveen and Rajeev Maheshwari pleaded being out of station on official work, which the court expressly said it was not at all satisfied with. Counsel for A-155, A-163 to A-166 and A-170 to A-178 argued their clients' absence was covered by the court's own observations of 04.09.2019. Company representatives pleaded fever or being out of station; exemption was allowed for that day only, the court taking a lenient view while recording dissatisfaction with the grounds.
2019-10-19_1: Routine - exemption applications only (fever, diarrhoea, lung infection, pending High Court remedy). One contested: exemption sought because the accused had approached the High Court was strongly opposed by SFIO. Notice under s.446 CrPC continued against a surety's identifier who claimed he had merely signed the bonds.
2019-11-02_1: Routine - exemption applications only (duties as a senior executive at DLF, a meeting at Chennai, viral fever, an unwell infant). Two contested: the exemption sought on the ground of a pending High Court remedy was strongly opposed by SFIO, as was the viral-fever plea of A-147. A-141 pleaded non-supply of documents.
2019-11-22_1: Largely exemption applications (a nephew's wedding at Jodhpur, an unwell infant, vertigo, pending High Court remedy, non-supply of documents). Substantive point: on the permanent exemption applications of A-180 and A-181, the court reasoned that no effective proceedings were being conducted because the case remained at the summoning stage, and exempted them till further orders, impressing on counsel that he must appear on every date.
2019-12-17_1: Routine - exemption applications (pending High Court remedy, non-supply of documents, pending anticipatory bail). The court declined the application for cancellation of a warrant of arrest and directed the prosecutor to supply complete and correct addresses within 7 days before fresh bailable warrants issued.
2020-01-31_1: Mostly exemption. One reasoned grant: A-154 Bharat Kumar Mardia, A-156 Praveen Maheshwari and A-157 Rajeev Maheshwari sought exemption till further orders on the ground that they reside in different places, carry on business across India, and the case is only at the initial stage of appearance. Orally opposed. Court allowed it and exempted them till further orders.
2020-09-24_1: Routine - exemption. Vijay Jindal (A-175) sought exemption on the ground that he was being admitted to AIIMS Delhi and could not attend because of COVID-19. Refused: his anticipatory bail had been dismissed by this court and no protection had been granted by the High Court.
2021-01-15_1: Routine - exemption. Vijay Shukla (A-149) sought exemption because he had gone to Chandigarh in connection with his anticipatory bail; dismissed, that application having been refused here and no protection subsisting.
2021-01-18_1: Counsel for Surender Singh (A-140) said he could not assist and sought adjournment as his senior was unavailable, having filed only a medical certificate and no treatment record. Court adjourned but directed the issuing or treating doctor to produce the record through a person conversant with the accused's condition.
2021-01-21_1: On the medical condition of Surender Singh (A-140). Counsel explained the hospital's staff were stuck in a traffic jam near Masani because of the Kisan Andolan and undertook to email the record. Dr Viratveer Yadav deposed by video conferencing that the accused had been infected with COVID-19, was on intermittent BiPAP support with severe pulmonary fibrosis, but was recovering well and could be moved in 10-15 days, adding that moving him sooner would be against medical advice. SFIO had no objection. Court directed he be shifted to District Jail, Bhondsi after ten days, with liberty to SFIO to have his condition verified by a Medical Board.
2021-02-02_1: Counsel submitted that the presence of A-179, A-182 and A-185 on 15.01.2021 had been omitted; the attendance sheet bore them out and the earlier order was corrected. On production of the High Court order of 28.01.2021 in CRM No.24870/2020, the court directed that no coercive action be taken against Vijay Shukla (A-149) on the non-bailable warrant or otherwise.
2021-02-19_1: Mostly exemption. Reasoned grant: Paramvir Singh Sangwan (A-174) sought exemption till further orders on the ground that he is 74 years old, suffers from various age-related illnesses, and faced a high risk of COVID-19 infection. Counsel for A-149 relied on High Court protection against coercive methods. The jails reported the accused had been taken on police remand by the Rajasthan police.
2021-03-05_1: SFIO sought a date for recording the approver statements of A-150 and A-158 because the Investigating Officer was unavailable and their proposed evidence had to be considered by him before submissions. Allowed; all scheduled approver dates deferred.
2021-04-16_1: The jail authorities submitted Virender Modi (A-122) could not be produced because he was on interim bail till 17.04.2021, and that Rahul and Mukesh Modi could not be produced from Jodhpur for want of escort, the Superintendent regretting the inconvenience. Court observed pointedly that it had never granted Virender Modi any such bail and that, being in custody in this case, he was legally bound to be produced; it required the Jodhpur authorities to explain the circumstances in which he was released on interim bail.
2021-08-04_2: Court's own correction. Noting that the predecessor had, with reasons, directed warrants of arrest on 04.09.2019 against fifteen named accused, it corrected its order of even date so that they be summoned by warrant of arrest rather than bailable warrant - bailable process having yielded no result in their case.
2021-08-17_1: Interim bail on the Supreme Court's reasoning. That court held that, having granted interim bail to the principal accused Vivek Harivyasi on 17.12.2020, Raj Kumar Modi likewise deserved release on interim bail on such terms as the trial court might impose. This court read the order as granting interim bail without any time limit, subsisting until the Supreme Court directed otherwise.
2021-09-08_1: DRI, through its Senior Special Public Prosecutor, applied for permission to enquire under s.108 of the Customs Act 1962 from Jainam Madhukant Rathore (A-130). A representative was allowed to appear for a company on the strength of an authority letter and resolution. The order also records that ten accused had been granted High Court bail on the condition that they cooperate with the prosecution as approvers.
2021-09-15_2: A genuine legal contest. Sudhir Mehta (A-170) applied under s.70(2) CrPC to recall the arrest warrants, relying on Aman Preet Singh v. CBI and Siddharth v. State of U.P. to argue that his arrest was unnecessary and his case squarely covered. The Special Prosecutor replied that his anticipatory bail was already pending before the High Court - a fact concealed in the application - so it was not maintainable here, and that the benefit of the cited law was not available to an accused summoned for offences punishable under the Companies Act, which is a special statute having prevailing impact over the general law. Court dismissed it on concealment alone, and held additionally that with the High Court seized of the matter and no interim stay granted, it could not entertain the request.
2021-09-15_4: Travel permission, contested only half-heartedly. Raj Kumar Bohra (A-171) set out his compliance history: passport deposited on 06.10.2020, permission to travel to UAE and Bangladesh granted on 23.11.2020 against Rs.1 crore security, returned before 14.01.2021, and attendance marked on 15.01.2021 and 19.02.2021. He argued he was not a flight risk and there was no apprehension of his evading trial, and sought to be excused from depositing his passport at every hearing with the existing surety treated as continuing. SFIO opposed orally and half-heartedly, not disputing that earlier permissions had been complied with. Permission granted on the Rs.1 crore security and itinerary conditions.
2021-09-17_1: DRI submitted that its investigation into evasion of customs duty against M/s Shivani Network and Jainam Madhukant Rathod alias Jainam Jain was at an advanced stage and sought permission for three named officers to make enquiries under s.108 of the Customs Act 1962, carrying their departmental records. Permitted; the jail directed to allow the visit on 21.09.2021.
2021-09-22_2: The most fully argued order in the set - 25 pages. Rajeev Kumar Rana (A-177) sought cancellation of the arrest warrant, arguing that he was never arrested during the investigation, which he had joined and cooperated with, and that under Siddharth v. State of U.P. and Aman Preet Singh v. CBI he could not be arrested now; he also relied on anticipatory bail granted to comparable accused by the Allahabad High Court and the Supreme Court, including to a co-accused in this very complaint. The Special Prosecutor replied that the case is governed by a special statute, that the application was not maintainable as anticipatory bail had been refused on 04.09.2019 and the challenge withdrawn on 01.10.2019, and that the court must additionally satisfy itself of the special statute's requirements over and above the CrPC. Court framed the question as whether non-arrest during investigation entitles an accused to immunity once process has issued, where anticipatory bail was refused and he has not appeared despite warrants. It held Aman Preet Singh and Siddharth distinguishable - neither dealt with s.212(6) of the Companies Act 2013, Aman Preet Singh turning on s.170 CrPC in an IPC case and Siddharth on anticipatory bail outside the Companies Act - and dismissed the application as a misuse of process seeking relief available only to an accused already on bail.
2021-10-30_1: Interim bail on the Supreme Court's reasoning: it found prima facie force in the submission that the loan was taken by the company seven years before the petitioner became a director, that he was merely an authorised signatory to a 2017 document, that co-accused had already been granted interim bail, and that he had been in custody since 2019. Before this court, counsel explained the surety could not immediately produce an FDR and offered Rs.1,00,000 in cash; the court allowed the cash deposit with liberty to substitute an FDR and claim refund.
2022-03-25_1: The order that opened proclamation proceedings, and the court's reasoning is repeated accused by accused: on each, 'this court is satisfied that the accused is intentionally avoiding his arrest and concealing oneself to prevent prosecution, thus to procure his presence proclamation is required under section 82 Cr.P.C.' Counsel for Abhay K. Shah asked the court not to proceed because his prayer was pending before the High Court; the court noted there was no stay of these proceedings and proceeded anyway. Ten accused granted High Court bail on the condition of cooperating as approvers were directed to appear for their statements.
2022-04-02_1: Court allowed four accused to become approvers, relying on the contents of their applications, the High Court's order made while granting them bail, and their statements on oath, and recording that it had original jurisdiction to entertain the complaint as a Special Court under s.306 CrPC.
2022-05-07_1: Two contested applications, both dismissed. Aditya Sarda (A-141) sought exemption for the day; the complainant opposed and the court dismissed it because a proclamation had already issued against him. Nitin Rathore (A-116) applied for Section 82 proceedings not to be launched; also opposed and dismissed, proclamation having already been ordered on 25.03.2022.
2022-05-11_1: SFIO applied for a fresh proclamation against Akshat Singh (A-136) on the ground that the police summons staff had never received one. The Ahlmad's report revealed the Naib Court had, in the court's words, played dirty by withholding or destroying the publication notice handed to him on 30.04.2022, so no proclamation had in fact issued. Fresh proclamation ordered; the court refrained from further action against the official pending the Commissioner of Police's enquiry.
2022-05-30_1: The Naib Court explained that the executing official had filed the proclamation report in the morning, left for another court, then fell ill and went to the Civil Hospital, a prescription slip being placed on record. The proclamation having been effected, the court merely deferred his statement.
2022-06-02_1: Meenakshi Modi (A-132) and Neha Ghemawat Modi (A-124) applied for non-bailable warrants not to issue, on the ground that the Supreme Court had by its order of 20.05.2022 in SLP (Crl.) Nos.4732-4733 of 2022 stayed the operation of the Rajasthan High Court order on which the warrants rested. Court accepted this and directed that warrants not issue, and be recalled unexecuted if already issued.
2022-07-02_1: Several accused resisted proclamation on the footing that other proceedings were pending. Proclamation against Shiv Raj Sharma was adjourned given the pendency in the High Court and, separately, his anticipatory bail here; the same for Naveen Kumar (A-139). Peeyush Aggarwal (A-173) applied to keep Section 82 proceedings in abeyance. Warrants against Meenakshi Modi and Neha Ghemawat Modi stood recalled on the Supreme Court's order. Exemptions for the day allowed to A-106, A-112, A-159 and A-178. Five approvers directed to appear for their statements.
2022-07-08_1: Megha Chauhan (A-163) sought return of her passport, on affidavit, to produce before the passport authority for renewal of her minor child Yashas's passport. SFIO did not oppose outright but asked that she be required to return it within a fixed period and that it be released against adequate surety. Court found the reason genuine, released the passport on a personal bond of Rs.50,000 with surety, required its return within one month, and made clear that release did not permit her to leave India.
2022-07-08_2: Raj Kumar Bohra (A-171) sought travel permission on affidavit: an NRI whose wife and three children live in Dubai, his wife suffering severe depression, UAE his primary place of business as managing partner of RKC International General Trading LLC with major export business in Bangladesh, and a record of returning on time. SFIO endorsed no objection on the margin. Permission granted against Rs.1 crore security.
2022-07-27_2: Contested proclamation proceedings. For Siddharth Chauhan (A-135), counsel produced the High Court's order of 01.07.2022 in CRM-M-27904-2022, in which senior counsel had relied on an earlier order of 24.05.2022 adjourning proclamation proceedings beyond the date fixed, and the High Court directed the case be listed before the same Bench after orders from the Chief Justice; proclamation here was adjourned. Shiv Raj Sharma's proceedings likewise adjourned pending the High Court. Peeyush Aggarwal's (A-173) wife and counsel undertook that he would appear within a week and prayed he not be declared a proclaimed person; the court, holding that the object of proclamation is to secure appearance, granted that time.
2022-08-30_2: Raj Kumar Bohra's travel application on the same grounds - NRI status, family in UAE, business obligations, and a record of timely return. SFIO endorsed no objection. The surety confirmed by affidavit that he would continue and produce the accused. Permission granted on the Rs.1 crore security.
2022-08-30_3: Counsel for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) produced the High Court's orders of 04.08.2022 and 25.08.2022 in CRM-M-27904-2022 and sought adjournment of proclamation; allowed. Peeyush Aggarwal (A-173) having filed an anticipatory bail application that day, the court held it was not appropriate to declare him a proclaimed person and kept proclamation in abeyance subject to that decision. Exemptions for the day allowed to A-107, A-112, A-116, A-127, A-141, A-160, A-163 and A-164. Six approvers directed to appear.
2022-10-18_2: Raj Kumar Bohra's travel application, same grounds, SFIO endorsing no objection, surety continuing; permission granted on the Rs.1 crore security with the surety's statement separately recorded.
2022-10-18_3: Two contested applications. An application under s.317 CrPC for appearance through pleader was vehemently opposed by the prosecutor on the ground that anticipatory bail had been dismissed both here and by the High Court, and was dismissed. On Peeyush Aggarwal's (A-173) application under s.205 CrPC, counsel contended that he was not running from the law and his having applied for anticipatory bail before the High Court showed he was abiding by it; the prosecutor opposed. Court observed that many SFIO anticipatory bail matters were pending before the High Court and that the prosecutor's argument could not be accepted at that stage, keeping Section 82 proceedings in abeyance pending the High Court's orders.
2022-12-09_2: Routine - exemption applications, all allowed on their stated grounds (A-117, A-150, A-163, A-164, A-171, A-179, A-180). Five approvers directed to appear for their statements on 08.02.2023.
2023-02-08_2: Routine - exemption applications allowed for the day. Counsel for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) again produced the High Court's orders of 04.08.2022 and 25.08.2022 and obtained adjournment of proclamation. Five approvers directed to appear on 03.04.2023.
2023-04-03_2: Exemptions allowed for the day. Counsel for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) produced the High Court's order of 27.03.2023 in CRM-M-27904-2022 recording that the proclamation adjournment remained in force, and proclamation was adjourned again. The substantive event is the dropping of proclamation proceedings against twelve accused who had obtained High Court bail and furnished bonds.
2023-05-22_1: The SFIO prosecutor contended that the applicant had been summoned by the order of 11.07.2019 and that, if he disclosed the true facts, the prosecution had no objection to his statement being recorded under s.306 CrPC. Counsel for the accused contended he was ready to disclose the true facts about the commission of the crime. Court examined s.306 and the High Court's order, satisfied itself on his willingness to make a full and true disclosure of every circumstance within his knowledge as to every person principal or abettor, allowed the application, and warned him that deviation would attract s.308 CrPC and that non-cooperation could result in custody.
2023-05-22_2: Same contentions and same order as the preceding entry - this is a duplicate publication of the 22.05.2023 approver order, its pages repeated within one PDF.
2023-05-30_2: Routine - exemptions, the prosecutor endorsing 'no objection for today only'. Counsel for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) produced the High Court's order of 18.05.2023 in CRM-M-27904-2022 recording the proclamation adjournment in force; proclamation adjourned again.
2023-08-29_1: Routine - exemptions allowed for the day. Counsel for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) again relied on the High Court's order of 18.05.2023 to keep proclamation adjourned.
2024-02-09_1: Routine - exemptions allowed for the day, and the same High Court order relied on for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135). The substantive step is the court's own: Shinder Pal Singh (A-137) having repeatedly failed to appear with notices returned unexecuted, proclamation under s.82 CrPC was ordered.
2024-05-03_1: Exemptions allowed, some till further orders. On Shiv Raj Sharma's (A-160) application under s.306 CrPC to become an approver, the prosecutor filed no reply and stated no objection, and the application was allowed on that footing. Shinder Pal Singh (A-137) was declared a proclaimed person after failing to appear by 3 p.m. with the mandatory thirty days expired.
2024-05-03_2: Raj Kumar Bohra's travel application on the familiar grounds - NRI, family in UAE, prior compliance. The surety confirmed by affidavit that he had already furnished Rs.1 crore security and would continue. The court noted his consistent compliance with every earlier permission and allowed it.
2024-06-04_1: Jainam Rathod (A-130) applied in person to deposit his passport and have released the Rs.2 lakh FDR furnished as security when the passport was released. Allowed; passport taken on record and the FDR returned against receipt.
2024-07-29_1: Proclamation against Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) adjourned again, the prosecutor stating that some interim order had been passed by the High Court but its latest status was unavailable. Court directed the accused to bring a certified copy of any order in his favour, failing which it would proceed as per law.
2024-09-03_1: The clearest statement of the approvers' status. Ten accused had applied to become approvers and their applications were allowed on 02.04.2022 and 22.05.2023, but no order making them witnesses was passed when pardon was tendered, so their names still appeared in the array of accused. Court held that as settled law, once an accused is granted pardon he ceases to be an accused and becomes a prosecution witness, and directed SFIO to include them in the list of witnesses, relieving them of attendance except when specifically directed during evidence.
2024-11-13_1: Proceedings against Virender Modi (A-122) recorded as abated. Arguments on two applications for permanent exemption, and on a further application, were deferred, counsel seeking adjournment.
2025-01-18_1: Two substantial contests. For Neha Ghemawat (A-124) and Meenakshi Modi (A-132), counsel traced the history: interim relief against coercive action granted 20.12.2019, later declined continuation by the Rajasthan High Court, whereupon the Supreme Court by order of 20.05.2022 in SLP (Crl.) 4732-4733/2022 asked that court to decide the writs within three months and continued the interim relief meanwhile; counsel argued that with that protection subsisting no further order need be produced. The Senior Prosecutor did not refute the history but submitted the protection was against coercive action by the investigating agency only, with no restraint on court proceedings. Court directed them to produce any restraint order on joining proceedings, failing which they must appear or face coercive steps. On SFIO's application to declare Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) a proclaimed person, his High Court petition having been dismissed as withdrawn on 09.01.2025, he sought adjournment to pursue a remedy; the court held that at least thirty days must be given in compliance with the publication effected on 30.04.2022 and adjourned accordingly.
2025-02-27_1: SFIO pressed for Siddharth Chauhan (A-135) to be declared a proclaimed person: his anticipatory bail petition CRM-M-8166-2025 was dismissed as withdrawn on 25.02.2025, the earlier petition dismissed as withdrawn on 09.01.2025, proclamation was already effected on 30.04.2022 and merely kept in abeyance, and he had full knowledge yet deliberately stayed away. Court held the application misconceived and liable to be rejected on propriety grounds: since the proclamation had been in abeyance, a sufficient period of at least thirty days had to be allowed, and it fixed 07.04.2025. On the s.88 CrPC / s.91 BNSS application of A-124 and A-132, the Senior Prosecutor argued it was not maintainable when the applicants would not appear; the court found force in that, observing they were clearly defying repeated directions without justifiable reason, but as a matter of abundant caution issued fresh summons.
2025-09-19_1: A pointed order on jail administration. Mukesh Modi (A-113), in custody in this case at Jodhpur, had been released on interim bail obtained in a Rajasthan case while his regular bail here remained pending before the High Court; the Superintendent's report having been unsatisfactory, the court directed the Home Secretary, Government of Rajasthan to obtain and submit a report on the lapses and delinquent behaviour of the Superintendent. Two accused applied to postpone proceedings and fresh non-bailable warrants pending their quashing petition CRM-M-32075-2025; the court held that absent any restraint order it could not distinguish them from similarly placed co-accused against whom coercive process had issued, particularly as the Supreme Court had directed such accused to surrender within a specified period and they had not complied.
